SECTION 1: USA HEAVY METAL LIMITS

Scope: Toys, Art Materials, Children’s Products, Child Care Articles
Target Age Group: 0–12 Years
Jurisdiction: United States of America (Federal + Key State Laws)
PART A: THE 8 FEDERALLY MANDATED SOLUBLE HEAVY METALS (ASTM F963-23)
Federal law requires testing for "soluble migration" of these 8 specific elements. This simulates what happens if a child swallows the material and it dissolves in stomach acid (0.07M HCl).
⚠️ CRITICAL RULE: If a material exceeds the soluble limit for any of these 8 elements, the product FAILS ASTM F963 and cannot be legally sold as a children's toy or art material in the USA.
PART B: TOTAL HEAVY METAL CONTENT LIMITS (CPSIA & 16 CFR)
Unlike "soluble" limits, "Total" limits measure the absolute amount of the metal in the entire material, regardless of whether it can dissolve. This is strictly enforced by the CPSC.
⚠️ CRITICAL RULE: The 90 ppm limit for lead in paint/surface coatings is absolute. There are no exceptions for children's products. Exceeding this triggers an automatic recall.
PART C: STATE-SPECIFIC HEAVY METAL LIMITS (STRICTER THAN FEDERAL)
If you sell in these states, you must meet BOTH federal limits AND these stricter state limits.

📚 SECTION A: EN 71-3 MIGRATION LIMITS ( EU HEAVY METAL RULEBOOK)
Jurisdiction: European Union (Toy Safety Directive 2009/48/EC)
Standard: EN 71-3:2019+A2:2024 (Latest version, effective June 2025)

Core Philosophy: The EU does not just test "Total Content" (like the US). It tests Migration—meaning how much of the element dissolves in simulated stomach acid (0.07M HCl, pH ~2) over 2 hours at 37°C. This simulates a child swallowing or mouthing the product [[8]].
📌 PART 1: THE 3 MATERIAL CATEGORIES (CRITICAL FOR R&D)
The limits change drastically based on the physical state of the material. Your AI must classify the user's product into one of these three categories first [[19]].
📌 PART 2: THE EXACT 19-ELEMENT MIGRATION LIMITS TABLE (EN 71-3:2019+A2:2024)
*All limits are in mg/kg (ppm). If a lab test result exceeds any of these numbers for the corresponding category, the product FAILS and is illegal to sell in the EU [[2]].*
⚠️ AI R&D LOGIC RULE: If a user inputs: "Product: Slime. Ingredient: Borax (Sodium Borate). Concentration: 2% (20,000 ppm)"

AI MUST OUTPUT: FAIL. Slime is Category II. The Boron limit is 300 ppm. 20,000 ppm is 66x over the legal limit. This will cause reproductive/developmental toxicity. Suggest replacement: Use guar gum or xanthan gum + saline solution instead of borax.
📌 PART 3: THE EXACT LAB TEST METHODOLOGY (HOW TO FORMULATE TO PASS)
R&D must understand how the test is done to engineer formulations that pass. Encapsulation and particle size matter [[11]].
Sample Preparation:
Category I & III: Material is cut into pieces as close to 6 mm as possible, or scraped into particles of ~0.5 mm [[37]].
Category II: Liquid is mixed thoroughly.
The Simulant: The sample is submerged in 0.07 M Hydrochloric Acid (HCl), which simulates human gastric juice (pH ~2) [[11]].
The Extraction: The mixture is shaken at 37 ± 2 °C (body temperature) for 1 hour with shaking, followed by 1 hour without shaking (Total = 2 hours) [[8]].
Filtration: The solution is filtered through a 0.45 µm or 0.02 µm membrane filter to remove undissolved solids [[37]].
Analysis: The filtered liquid is analyzed using ICP-MS (Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry) to measure only the dissolved (migrated) elements [[38]].

💡 R&D FORMULATION HACK: If a pigment contains trace heavy metals, binding it tightly in a highly stable, non-soluble polymer matrix (like high-grade acrylic or silicone) can prevent it from dissolving in the 0.07M HCl, allowing it to pass the migration test even if the total content is slightly elevated. However, total content limits (REACH) still apply.

📚 SECTION B: EU REACH ANNEX XVII
Jurisdiction: European Union (EU)
Regulation: Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH), Annex XVII

Core Philosophy: REACH Annex XVII is an absolute ban or strict restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market, and use of specific dangerous substances. Unlike EN 71-3 (which tests migration), REACH tests Total Content in the material. Failing REACH means the product is illegal to sell in the EU, regardless of migration results.
📌 PART 1: ENTRY 43 — AZO DYES & AROMATIC AMINES (THE EXACT 22 LIST)
Azo dyes are widely used in textiles, leather, and colored art materials. Under certain conditions (e.g., in contact with skin or saliva), they can cleave and release carcinogenic aromatic amines.

The Rule: Shall not be used in textile and leather articles which may come into direct and prolonged contact with human skin (e.g., clothing, bedding, toys, footwear, gloves, wristbands) if they release any of the following 22 aromatic amines in concentrations > 30 mg/kg (30 ppm) in the tested parts [[12]].

📌 PART 2: ENTRY 50 & 50a — POLYCYCLIC AROMATIC HYDROCARBONS (PAHs) (THE EXACT 18 LIST)
PAHs are byproducts of incomplete combustion, often found in cheap rubber, recycled plastics, carbon black pigments, and extender oils.

The Rule: Articles supplied to the general public, toys, and childcare articles shall not be placed on the market if their rubber or plastic components that come into direct and prolonged or short-term repetitive contact with human skin or the oral cavity contain any of the listed PAHs above the specified limits [[68]].

⚠️ CRITICAL R&D RULE: For toys, the limit is 0.5 mg/kg (0.5 ppm) for each individual PAH. Furthermore, the sum of all 18 PAHs must not exceed 10 mg/kg in toys/childcare articles, or 50 mg/kg in clay targets [[44]].

The Rule: Substances classified as CMR Category 1A, 1B, or 2 shall not be used in clothing, textiles, or footwear (including toys with textile components) that come into contact with human skin to an extent similar to clothing, if the concentration of the substance is equal to or greater than the specified cut-off limits .

📚 SECTION C: EU CLP REGULATION (EC) No 1272/2008
Jurisdiction: European Union (EU)

Core Philosophy: The CLP Regulation aligns the EU with the UN’s Globally Harmonized System (GHS). For mixtures (formulations with multiple ingredients), you cannot just look at the final product; you must calculate the cumulative toxicity of all hazardous ingredients to determine the final hazard class, signal word, and mandatory label.
📌 PART 1: THE TWO PATHWAYS FOR MIXTURE CLASSIFICATION
Before calculating, the R&D model must determine which of the two legal pathways applies to the formulation.
📌 PART 2: GENERIC CUT-OFF VALUES (The Exact % Thresholds)
If a mixture contains a hazardous ingredient above a specific "Cut-Off" percentage, the entire mixture MUST be classified and labeled for that hazard. These are the absolute legal triggers.

⚠️ CRITICAL R&D RULE: If your liquid paint contains 5% Toluene (Acute Tox Cat 4), it crosses the 1.0% threshold. The entire paint must now carry the "WARNING" signal word and the "Harmful if swallowed" label, even if the other 95% is perfectly safe water and acrylic.
📌 PART 3: SPECIFIC M-FACTORS (The Override Rule)
The EU assigns "Multipliers" (M-factors) to the most toxic chemicals. If an ingredient has an M-factor, it overrides the generic cut-off values above. This makes the limit much stricter.

How it works: If a chemical has an M-factor of 10, the cut-off value is divided by 10. Example: For Acute Tox Cat 1, the generic cut-off is 0.1%. If the chemical has an M-factor of 10, the cut-off becomes 0.01% (100 ppm).

💡 R&D FORMULATION HACK: Always check the ECHA C&L Inventory for the specific M-factor of your raw materials. Using a chemical with an M-factor of 100 means you can only use it at trace levels (<10 ppm) before triggering a "DANGER" label on the final product.
📌 PART 4: THE ADDITIVITY FORMULA (Calculating Acute Toxicity)

If a mixture contains multiple ingredients that cause Acute Toxicity, you cannot just add their percentages together. You must calculate the ATE (Acute Toxicity Estimate) of the mixture using this exact mathematical formula mandated by CLP Annex II.
The Formula: 100 / ATE(mix) = Sum of [ (C(i) / ATE(i)) ]
Where:
ATE(mix) = The Acute Toxicity Estimate of the final mixture (the number you are trying to find).
C(i) = The concentration percentage of ingredient "i" in the mixture.
ATE(i) = The Acute Toxicity Estimate of ingredient "i" (found on its Safety Data Sheet, usually expressed in mg/kg body weight for oral/dermal, or mg/L for inhalation).
How to interpret the ATE(mix) result: Once you calculate the ATE(mix), you compare it to the CLP category boundaries:
If ATE(mix) is ≤ 5 mg/kg (Oral) -> Mixture is Category 1 (DANGER)
If ATE(mix) is > 5 and ≤ 50 mg/kg (Oral) -> Mixture is Category 2 (DANGER)
If ATE(mix) is > 50 and ≤ 300 mg/kg (Oral) -> Mixture is Category 3 (DANGER)
If ATE(mix) is > 300 and ≤ 2000 mg/kg (Oral) -> Mixture is Category 4 (WARNING)
If ATE(mix) is > 2000 mg/kg -> Mixture is Not Classified for Acute Toxicity.
📌 PART 5: THE SUMMATION METHOD (Skin/Eye & STOT)

For hazards like Skin Corrosion, Eye Damage, and Specific Target Organ Toxicity (STOT), you use the Summation Method. You add up the percentages of the hazardous ingredients and apply specific multipliers.
Example: Calculating Skin Corrosion / Irritation
Sum the % of all ingredients classified as Skin Corrosion Cat 1A/1B. If the sum is ≥ 1.0%, the mixture is Skin Corrosion Cat 1.
If not, sum the % of all ingredients classified as Skin Corrosion Cat 1C. If the sum is ≥ 5.0%, the mixture is Skin Corrosion Cat 1.
If not, sum the % of all Skin Corrosion Cat 1 ingredients PLUS 10 times the % of all Skin Irritation Cat 2 ingredients. If the sum is ≥ 10.0%, the mixture is Skin Irritation Cat 2.
📌 PART 6: MANDATORY WARNING LABELS (Pictograms, Signal Words, H & P Statements)
Once the hazard class is calculated, the exact label elements are strictly mandated. You cannot choose which ones to print; you must print ALL that apply.
1. GHS Pictograms (The 9 Red Diamond Symbols)
2. Signal Words
Only one signal word can appear on the label. "Danger" overrides "Warning".
DANGER: Used for severe hazards (Acute Tox Cat 1-3, Skin Corr 1, Eye Dam 1, Carcinogen Cat 1A/1B, etc.).
WARNING: Used for less severe hazards (Acute Tox Cat 4, Skin Irrit 2, Eye Irrit 2, Aquatic Tox, etc.).
3. Hazard (H) and Precautionary (P) Statements
H-Statements (The Risk): e.g., H302 (Harmful if swallowed), H315 (Causes skin irritation), H332 (Harmful if inhaled), H304 (May be fatal if swallowed and enters airways).

P-Statements (The Safety): e.g., P102 (Keep out of reach of children), P301+P310 (IF SWALLOWED: Immediately call a POISON CENTER/doctor), P305+P351+P338 (IF IN EYES: Rinse continuously with water for several minutes).
📌 PART 7: CHILD-RESISTANT CLOSURES & TACTILE WARNINGS
This is where CLP intersects with physical packaging. If a mixture is hazardous, the physical bottle must be engineered to prevent child access.
Triggers for Child-Resistant Fastenings (CRF) & Tactile Warnings (Raised Triangle): Under CLP and the Poisons Packaging directives, if a mixture supplied to the general public is classified as:
Acute Toxicity (Oral, Dermal, or Inhalation) Category 1, 2, or 3.
Specific Target Organ Toxicity (STOT) Category 1.
Aspiration Hazard Category 1 (e.g., mineral spirits, turpentine).
Contains Methanol (Acute Tox Cat 3) in concentrations ≥ 3%.
Mandatory Physical Requirements:
The container MUST have a Child-Resistant Closure (CRC) that passes ISO 8317 testing (85% of children aged 42-51 months cannot open it in 5 minutes, while 90% of adults can).
The container MUST bear a Tactile Warning of Danger (a raised equilateral triangle with a black border and black exclamation mark, minimum 20mm height) so visually impaired users can feel the hazard.
📌 PART 8: THE "TOY VS. ART MATERIAL" CLP PARADOX (CRITICAL R&D RULE)
This is the most common trap for manufacturers selling in the EU. You must understand how CLP interacts with the Toy Safety Directive (TSD).
The Paradox: Under the EU Toy Safety Directive (2009/48/EC), a product cannot be classified as a "toy" if it is classified as "hazardous" under the CLP Regulation.

If your formulation calculates to a CLP Hazard Class (e.g., Aspiration Hazard Cat 1, or Acute Tox Cat 4), it is legally banned from being sold as a toy. No amount of child-resistant packaging will save it. It must be recalled or reformulated.
The Solution for R&D:

If the product is for Children (<14 years): It MUST be a toy. Therefore, the CLP calculation must result in "Not Classified" for all physical and health hazards. You must reformulate to remove all aspiration hazards, acute toxins, and corrosives.

If the product is for Adults/Teens (e.g., professional acrylics, model making paints): It can be classified as an "Art Material" rather than a toy. In this case, it CAN carry CLP hazard labels (Danger/Warning, GHS pictograms), provided it has the correct child-resistant packaging and tactile warnings if it triggers those thresholds.
